description.narrative:
In 2020, Oxfam conducted a study titled Breaking the Localisation Deadlock, which examined the barriers to effective localisation in Somalia. The study focused on five key factors: Identity and Mission, Managerial Capacities, Approach and Commitment, Technical Expertise, and Size and Capability. It highlighted the growing capacity of local and national NGOs (LNNGOs) and government agencies, while also noting the dominance of international NGOs (INGOs) and UN agencies in the humanitarian landscape.
The 2024 research initiative builds on this foundation, aiming to explore the progress and emerging trends in localisation. Specifically, it will focus on the inclusion of LNNGOs in the coordination and leadership of the 2023-2024 humanitarian responses to drought and floods. This research aligns with Oxfam’s broader mission to promote equitable and inclusive humanitarian responses that prioritise local leadership and community involvement. Given the ongoing humanitarian challenges in Somalia, particularly exacerbated by the severe drought and floods, understanding the role of local actors is crucial to ensuring that responses are not only effective but also equitable.
The primary audience for this research includes: • Local and national NGOs operating in Somalia. • INGOs and UN agencies involved in humanitarian efforts. • Government agencies responsible for disaster response and recovery. • Donors and funding organisations interested in supporting localised humanitarian initiatives. • Other key regional and global stakeholders promoting localisation. • Academicand research institutions analysing humanitarian practices.
The findings aim to inform strategic planning within the Oxfam Somali Programme and other humanitarian actors, helping to improve the operationalisation of localisation commitments and ultimately enhancing the effectiveness of future humanitarian responses in Somalia. Additionally, the research seeks to contribute to the broader discourse on localisation and gender inclusion in humanitarian action, both in Somalia and beyond.
The study has several key objectives: 1. Evaluating the extent to which the recommendations from the 2020 Breaking the Localisation Deadlock study were implemented in the 2023–2024 drought and flood responses by local actors, including LNNGOs and government agencies. 2. Assessing progress toward achieving more inclusive coordination and leadership within Somalia's humanitarian system.
Gender will be a central focus of this research, which will adopt a gender-transformative approach to assess progress toward more inclusive decision-making processes in recent humanitarian responses. The consultancy will focus particularly on identifying innovative practices for inclusive humanitarian response in Somalia. The primary goal is to identify innovations in ways of working and decision-making, but it may also include improvements in the efficiency of aid delivery, especially for those at higher risk of exclusion, such as marginalised communities, peoplewith disabilities, and women-headed households. The research process will encourage the use of both visual and narrative methods indeveloping case studies.

participating-org.narrative: In 2004 Oxfam Novib set up a Liaison Office in Nairobi, Kenya in order to support the Strengthening Somali Civil Society Program, at the request of the EU. This request was based on Oxfam Novib's work in Somalia to date, but intended to be more widely directed atthe entire civil society sector and the specific context in which it is operating in a post-conflict country. The program started with consulting local organisations in Somalia and Somaliland to get a complete picture of the sectors and regions where they are active, the challenges they face and the relationship between civil society, local political structures and the private sector. A program was then developed to strengthen the institutional development of Oxfam Novib's partners and those of other Oxfams, as well as a range of new NGOs. In the first year local consultants were trained in Somalia. They were then seconded to civil society organisations to build their capacity in financial and organisational management. Furthermore, workshops were organised on specific themes suchas human rights and the role of civil society in the Somali context. The Liaison Office is now going to support the expansion of the program, focussing on strengthening both organisation and project management, while facilitating more training in the fields of civic education, governance, human rights and women's rights, HIV and AIDS and child protection. Over the years, the Somalia Country Office has expanded its intervention on short term humanitarian response as well as development development interventions. In 2015/2016, a decision was reached to move the Country Programme operation, which was largely in Nairobi, from Nairobi to Hargeisa. The country office has a small office in Nairobi , Kenya and large operations office in Hargeisa, Somaliland.
